title: Quantum Quantitative Trading: High-Frequency Statistical Arbitrage Algorithm
abstract_summary: The paper proposes quantum algorithms for high-frequency statistical arbitrage by combining variable-time condition number estimation and quantum linear regression to accelerate preselection and cointegration testing of candidate portfolios. It introduces a Quantum Condition Number Comparison/Estimation tool and a Quantum Cointegration Test (QCT), claiming complexity reductions from classical O(N^2 d) to roughly O(√d κ0^2 log(1/ε)^2) under certain assumptions and demonstrating potential quantum advantage for large high-frequency datasets.
methodology_description: This theoretical work develops quantum algorithms for high-frequency statistical arbitrage by combining condition-number based preselection with quantum-enabled cointegration verification. The authors introduce a Variable Time Preselection Algorithm (VTPA) that uses a Quantum Condition Number Comparison/Comparator subroutine (QCNCA/QCNC) based on repeated phase-estimation-style tests to detect small eigenvalues (hence large condition numbers) in design matrices; the QCNCA is used as a filter to rapidly discard well-conditioned portfolios. VTPA implements a multi-stage (clock-register) conditional sequence of QCNC calls (Aj stages) with a stop flag to adaptively test progressively larger condition-number thresholds and exploit a variable-time speedup. For cointegration verification they propose a Quantum Cointegration Test (QCT) that leverages a Quantum Linear Regression (QLR) primitive (building on HHL/WBL/SSP/Wang-style algorithms, qubitization and quantum signal processing ideas) to compute regression coefficients, constructs residuals via a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline (amplitude-encoded input via qRAM, quantum regression to obtain β, classical matrix multiplication and vector subtraction to compute residuals), computes lagged residuals and then runs a second QLR for the augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) style regression to obtain the test statistic which is evaluated classically against critical values. The methodology contains detailed complexity analyses and proofs (lemmas and theorems) for correctness and query/gate complexity under distributional assumptions on eigenvalues (uniform log-κ distribution used as an example). Key assumptions include availability of qRAM-style oracles for amplitude encoding of price matrices, access to unitary simulation of A = [0 X; X^T 0], balanced design matrices (singular values in [1/κ,1]), and bounds on desired precision ϵ and condition-number thresholds κ0. The paper is theoretical: it specifies algorithmic pipelines, oracle models, register layout (clock registers, flag, ancillas), and asymptotic complexity and error-propagation bounds rather than empirical/implementation experiments.
algorithms_used: Quantum Condition Number Comparison / Comparator (QCNCA / QCNC)
Quantum Linear Regression (QLR) (based on HHL / WBL / qubitization / Wang)

dataset_used: No empirical experiment. The paper discusses realistic high-frequency US equity market data as a motivating use case: half-second aggregated quotes over a 6.5-hour trading day (N0 = 46,800 samples/day), ~253 trading days per year, giving N ≈ 1.2 × 10^7 samples for one year; J ≈ 8000 stocks is used as a realistic universe. Data is assumed accessible via a qRAM-style oracle mapping |j>|t>|z> → |j>|t>|z xor p_jt> and amplitude-encoding for residual vectors.

[speculative] They present a complexity expression for the Quantum Cointegration Test (QCT) consisting of quantum linear regression and hybrid classical steps: roughly O(d^{2.5} κ^3 / δ^2 poly(log(d κ / δ)) + d N + (L+2)^{2.5} κ'^{3} / δ'^{2} poly(log((L+2) κ' / δ')) ), with δ and δ' defined in the paper.

results_summary: This preprint proposes a quantum approach to high-frequency statistical arbitrage by introducing (1) a Variable Time Preselection Algorithm (VTPA) that filters portfolios via a quantum condition-number testing subroutine (QCNCA/QCNC), and (2) a Quantum Cointegration Test (QCT) that combines quantum linear regression with classical residual computation and ADF testing. The paper derives theoretical complexity bounds for these subroutines, argues a potential polynomial speedup over a stated classical benchmark (especially for the preselection phase under certain distributional assumptions), and provides a realistic illustrative estimate for U.S. market data showing large gap between their claimed quantum complexity and classical cost. All results are analytical/theoretical and contingent on assumptions such as qRAM access, uniform-log-κ distributions, and efficient Hamiltonian simulation.
performance_claims: Classical benchmark for preselection (stated): O(N^2 d).
VTPA average query complexity (claimed under uniform-log-κ): O(sqrt(d) κ0^2 log(1/ϵ)^2).
QCNCA (QCNC) calls of A in uniform-eigenvalue case (claimed): O(κ0^2 log(1/ϵ)).
QCT total complexity (claimed): O(d^{2.5} κ^3 / δ^2 poly(log(d κ / δ)) + d N + (L+2)^{2.5} κ'^{3} / δ'^{2} poly(log((L+2) κ' / δ'))).

Realistic data parameters used: N ≈ 1.2 × 10^7 (half-second aggregation over 253 trading days), ~8000 stocks, pool of 3-stock portfolios M ≈ C(8000,3) ≈ 10^9, expected multicollinear set M0 ≲ 1000 (M0/M ≤ 10^{-6}).
Numerical illustrative claim: classical cost O(N^2 d) ≈ 10^{18} vs. claimed quantum preselection cost ≈ 10^{8} for κ0 = 1000.
Estimated qubit count (claimed): ~35 qubits to encode data plus extra registers; authors state 'more than 50 qubits' likely required.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper claims a theoretical quantum speedup (complexity reduction) for the preselection step and provides asymptotic complexity bounds and a realistic numerical illustration. The claim is theoretical/speculative: it relies on strong assumptions (efficient qRAM/oracle access, ability to simulate e^{iA} efficiently, and particular eigenvalue/condition-number distribution assumptions), and no empirical or simulated implementation or resource-demonstration is provided.
limitations: Algorithm complexity depends strongly on the matrix condition number κ; ill-conditioned matrices (large κ) increase resource cost significantly (authors discuss κ-dependence and need for κ0 threshold).
Assumption of uniform (or simple) eigenvalue / log-κ distributions for complexity analysis; complexity proofs rely on these distributional assumptions.
Algorithm uses the qRAM / oracle data-access model and amplitude encoding; practical qRAM construction and I/O overheads are not addressed.
The QCNCA/VTPA approach is described as heuristic — some cointegrated pairs may be missed (authors explicitly state some cointegrated pairs can be missed by the preselection).
Hybrid steps remain classical (matrix multiplication, ADF statistic calculation), so full end-to-end quantum speedup is partial and depends on classical subroutines.
No empirical evaluation or numerical experiments on real market data or noisy quantum hardware are provided (preprint presents theory only).
Resource estimates (qubit counts, gate depth) are coarse; implementation-level overheads, constant factors and fault-tolerance requirements are not quantified.
QLR and other subroutines require 'balanced' and 'well-behaved' inputs (e.g., singular values in [1/κ,1]); these preconditions may not hold for arbitrary market data.
Precision and error propagation are bounded but practical effects (e.g., accumulation under finite sampling, finite precision of price encoding) are not experimentally validated.
[inferred] Reliance on phase-estimation and Hamiltonian simulation primitives implies large circuit depth and fragility to noise on NISQ devices.
[inferred] The practical selection or estimation of the threshold κ0 (used for preselection) is not specified; choosing κ0 impacts both recall of cointegrated portfolios and runtime.
[inferred] Assumption that the proportion of multicollinear portfolios is tiny (M0/M ≪ 1) is used to argue speedup; this may not hold across markets or choices of d.
[inferred] Overheads of building and updating qRAM for streaming high-frequency data (latency/throughput constraints) are not addressed.
[inferred] The approach does not consider market frictions (transaction costs, slippage, latency) that can negate arbitrage profits in high-frequency trading.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Proposes a Variable Time Preselection Algorithm (VTPA) using a Quantum Condition Number Comparator (QCNCA/QCNC) that, under uniform-log-κ eigenvalue assumptions and qRAM access, yields asymptotic query complexity for preselection roughly O(√d κ0^2 log(1/ε)^2) versus a stated classical O(N^2 d) baseline, and provides a numerical illustrative gap (classical ~10^18 vs quantum ~10^8) for a U.S. HFT parameter set.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Designs a Quantum Cointegration Test (QCT) that combines quantum linear regression (HHL/qubitization-style) with classical residual computation to produce an ADF-style test statistic; derives end-to-end complexity expressions showing potential polynomial speedups subject to condition-number, precision and oracle assumptions.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Uses a hybrid pipeline: amplitude-encoded input via qRAM and quantum linear regression to obtain coefficients, followed by classical matrix multiplication/subtraction to compute residuals and classical evaluation of the test statistic (hybrid quantum-classical verification).

#idea:hybrid-approach — Introduces variable-time / multi-stage conditional testing (clock registers and stop flags) to exploit instances with favorable condition numbers and reduce average query complexity compared to naive repeated tests.
